title: Open Source vs Closed Source AI
readingMarkdown:
# Open Source vs Closed Source AI

"Is it open source?" sounds like a yes-or-no question. For AI models it is not. A model can be free to download and forbidden to use commercially. It can be usable commercially and impossible to inspect. It can be called "open" in a press release and fail every formal test of the word. This chapter gives you a precise vocabulary for what a vendor has actually released, a clear view of the trade-offs, and the practical skill of reading a license and a model card before you build on a model.

## 1. First-Principles Mental Model & Intuition

### Three ways to get dinner

Think about three ways to eat a restaurant's signature dish.

1. **Eat at the restaurant.** You order, the dish arrives, you pay per plate. You never see the kitchen or the recipe. The restaurant can change the menu, raise prices, or stop serving the dish, and it sees everything you order. This is an **API-only** model, also called closed.
2. **Buy the dish frozen.** You take the finished product home. You can reheat it whenever you like, add your own seasoning, and serve it without the restaurant knowing. You still do not have the recipe or the ingredient list, and the box may carry conditions such as "not for resale by large chains". This is an **open-weight** model.
3. **Get the recipe, the method, and a full account of the ingredients**, under terms that let you cook it, change it, and share your version. This is **open source** in the strict sense.

Most arguments about "open" AI come from people using the third label for the second thing.

### What is inside the box

To see why the distinction matters, recall what a trained model is made of.

```text
 +---------------------+   +---------------------+   +---------------------+
 |   TRAINING DATA     |   |   TRAINING CODE     |   |      WEIGHTS        |
 | what it learned     |   | how it was trained  |   | the result: billions|
 | from                |   | and how to run it   |   | of learned numbers  |
 +---------------------+   +---------------------+   +---------------------+
          |                          |                         |
          |                          |                         |
  usually NOT released        sometimes released       released for "open-weight"
                                                       models, never for API-only
```

With traditional software, releasing the source code gives you everything: you can read it, understand it, and rebuild the program. With an AI model, the **weights** alone do not do that. They let you *run* and *fine-tune* the model. They do not let you see what it was trained on, reproduce it, or fully audit it. That gap is the whole reason "open source" needed a new definition for AI.

### The four questions

For any model, ask in this order.

1. **What do I actually receive?** An API key, a weights file, or weights plus code plus information about the data.
2. **Under which license?** What am I permitted and forbidden to do with it.
3. **What will it cost to run?** Per token through an API, or hardware and staff if I host it.
4. **Who is accountable when it breaks?** A vendor with a support contract, or me.

The rest of the chapter works through each.

## 2. Core Theory, Mathematical Foundations & Architecture Internals

### The release ladder

| Rung | You receive | You can | You cannot |
|---|---|---|---|
| API-only (closed weights) | Network access to a hosted model | Send prompts, get outputs, sometimes fine-tune through the vendor | Run it yourself, inspect it, keep a version the vendor retires |
| Open weights | The parameter files, usually with inference code | Run it on your own hardware, fine-tune it, keep it forever | Necessarily use it for any purpose (depends on license); see or reproduce the training |
| Open source AI (strict) | Weights, complete training and inference code, and detailed information about the training data, all under approved terms | Use, study, modify, and share for any purpose | Nothing essential is withheld |

### The formal definition

The Open Source Initiative, the body that stewards the definition of open-source software, published version 1.0 of its **Open Source AI Definition (OSAID)** in late October 2024. It requires that an AI system grant four freedoms: to **use** it for any purpose, to **study** how it works, to **modify** it, and to **share** it. To make those freedoms real, three things must be available under suitable terms:

- **Data information.** Sufficiently detailed information about the training data that a skilled person could build a substantially equivalent system. Note what this says: a description of the data, its sources, and how it was processed, and not necessarily the data itself.
- **Code.** The complete source code used to train and run the system.
- **Parameters.** The model weights.

Measured against this, most well-known "open" models do not qualify. In its own review at the end of 2024 the OSI listed a few research models as compliant and named several famous model families as not compliant. The definition is itself debated, with critics on one side arguing that it should require the full training data and on the other that it is too strict to be useful. You do not have to take a side. You do need to know that **open weights is the accurate term for most models people call open source.**

The practice of marketing a restricted model as "open source" has a name: **openwashing**.

### License families

The license is a legal document that says what you may do. For models, four broad families cover most cases.

| Family | Examples | Commercial use | Notable conditions |
|---|---|---|---|
| Permissive open-source licenses | Apache 2.0, MIT | Yes | Keep the license and copyright notices. Apache 2.0 also includes an explicit patent grant |
| Custom "community" licenses | Meta's Llama licenses | Yes, with limits | Additional rules written by the vendor: usage policies, naming and attribution requirements, scale thresholds |
| Custom terms of use | Earlier Google Gemma terms | Yes, with limits | A prohibited-use policy that must be passed on to anyone you distribute to |
| Research or non-commercial | Various academic and preview releases | No | For study and experiments only |

Some concrete details, accurate at the time of writing and worth verifying against the current license text before you rely on them:

- The **Llama 4 Community License** from Meta permits commercial use but is not an open-source license. If your products had more than 700 million monthly active users, you must request a separate license from Meta. You must display "Built with Llama", derivative models must carry "Llama" at the start of their names, and the license incorporates an acceptable use policy.
- **Gemma** from Google was originally released under custom terms with a prohibited-use policy. The Gemma 4 release in 2026 is listed on its model card under Apache 2.0. This is a good lesson in itself: *licenses change between versions of the same model family.*
- Several model families from OpenAI (its gpt-oss models), Alibaba (Qwen), DeepSeek, and Mistral's smaller models have been released under Apache 2.0 or MIT. Not every model from those companies is: the largest and newest models from a vendor are often API-only.
- The flagship models behind ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini are API-only.

One point surprises people. A permissive license on the weights covers the weights and the code. It says nothing about whether the training data was properly licensed, and it gives you no rights in that data.

### The trade-offs

| Dimension | Hosted API (closed) | Self-hosted open weights |
|---|---|---|
| Cost structure | Pay per token, no fixed cost | Fixed cost for hardware and staff, low cost per token |
| Capability | Usually the most capable models available | Strong and improving, typically somewhat behind the frontier |
| Privacy | Your data goes to the vendor under its terms | Data can stay entirely on your machines |
| Control | Vendor can change or retire a model | You pin a version and keep it; you can fine-tune freely |
| Operations | Vendor handles scaling, updates, security | You handle all of it |
| Support | Service agreements and a support desk | Community forums unless you pay a third party |
| Offline use | Impossible | Possible |

There is a third option that mixes the columns: an open-weight model served by a hosting company. You get open weights and pay-per-token pricing, but your data again leaves your machines. "Open model" and "private" are separate properties.

### The break-even calculation

The cost question can be answered with one formula. Let:

- $F$ be the fixed monthly cost of self-hosting (GPU rental or amortised hardware, electricity, and the staff time to run it),
- $c_s$ be the marginal cost of self-hosting per million tokens,
- $c_a$ be the API price per million tokens, blended across input and output,
- $T$ be your monthly volume in millions of tokens.

Monthly cost of each option:

$$
\text{Cost}_{\text{API}} = c_a\,T \qquad\qquad \text{Cost}_{\text{self}} = F + c_s\,T
$$

Self-hosting is cheaper when $F + c_s T < c_a T$. Solving for the volume at which the two are equal gives the **break-even point**:

$$
T^{*} = \frac{F}{c_a - c_s}
$$

Below $T^{*}$ the API is cheaper. Above it self-hosting is cheaper. If $c_a \le c_s$ there is no break-even and the API always wins.

A worked example with illustrative numbers. Suppose a rented GPU server plus a share of an engineer's time costs USD 3,000 per month, the marginal cost of running it is USD 0.10 per million tokens, and the comparable API charges USD 2.00 per million tokens:

$$
T^{*} = \frac{3000}{2.00 - 0.10} \approx 1579 \text{ million tokens per month}
$$

That is roughly 1.6 billion tokens a month, or about 53 million tokens a day. A company processing a few million tokens a day is far below break-even and should use the API on cost grounds. A company processing hundreds of millions a day is far above it.

```text
 monthly
 cost
   |                                    API  (slope c_a)
   |                                  /
   |                                /
   |                              /        self-host (starts at F, slope c_s)
   |                    ________/_________--------
   |          ________--      / 
   |  F ____--              /
   |                      /
   |                    /
   +------------------+--------------------------- monthly tokens
                      T*  break-even
```

**Utilisation changes everything.** The fixed cost buys capacity whether you use it or not. If a server can produce $R$ million tokens per hour and costs $h$ per hour, its true cost per million tokens is:

$$
c_{\text{effective}} = \frac{h}{R \times u}
$$

where $u$ is utilisation, the fraction of time the server is doing useful work. At 10 percent utilisation each token costs ten times what it would at full load. Idle GPUs are the main reason self-hosting projects cost more than planned.

### Model cards

A **model card** is the documentation that accompanies a model. The idea comes from the 2018 paper "Model Cards for Model Reporting" by Margaret Mitchell and colleagues, which proposed that every released model state its intended uses, the conditions it was evaluated under, its performance across different groups of people, and its known limitations.

On the Hugging Face Hub, the largest public repository of models, the card is the repository's README file. It begins with a metadata header, followed by free text:

```text
---
license: apache-2.0
base_model: some-org/some-base-model
datasets:
  - some-org/some-dataset
library_name: transformers
pipeline_tag: text-generation
---
# Model name
## Intended use ...
## Limitations ...
## Training data ...
## Evaluation ...
```

Read a card in this order:

1. **`license`.** If it says `other`, the license is custom. Find `license_name` and `license_link` and read the actual text.
2. **Intended use and limitations.** What the authors say it is and is not for.
3. **`base_model`.** If this model is a fine-tune of another, the base model's license conditions usually still apply.
4. **Training data and evaluation.** What it learned from, and how it was tested.

A missing section is information too. A card with no license field and no description of the data is a warning.

## 3. Production-Grade Implementation & Annotated Walkthrough

The checks in this chapter are simple enough to encode. The following standard-library program implements the release ladder, a license check, and the break-even calculation.

```python
def classify_release(release):
    """Place a model on the release ladder from what the vendor actually published."""
    if not release.get("weights"):
        return "api-only"
    if release.get("code") and release.get("data_info") and release.get("osi_license"):
        return "open-source"
    return "open-weights"

LICENSES = {
    "apache-2.0":      {"commercial": True,  "mau_limit": None},
    "mit":             {"commercial": True,  "mau_limit": None},
    "llama-community": {"commercial": True,  "mau_limit": 700_000_000},
    "research-only":   {"commercial": False, "mau_limit": None},
}

def can_use(license_key, commercial, monthly_active_users):
    """Return (allowed, reason). Unknown licenses are never assumed to be fine."""
    terms = LICENSES.get(license_key)
    if terms is None:
        return False, "unknown license: read the full text"
    if commercial and not terms["commercial"]:
        return False, "commercial use is not permitted"
    if terms["mau_limit"] is not None and monthly_active_users > terms["mau_limit"]:
        return False, "above the monthly-active-user limit: request a license"
    return True, "ok"

def break_even_millions(fixed_monthly, self_cost_per_m, api_price_per_m):
    """Monthly volume (millions of tokens) above which self-hosting is cheaper."""
    if api_price_per_m <= self_cost_per_m:
        return None                      # the API is cheaper at every volume
    return fixed_monthly / (api_price_per_m - self_cost_per_m)

print(classify_release({"weights": True, "code": False, "data_info": False, "osi_license": True}))
print(can_use("research-only", commercial=True, monthly_active_users=10_000))
print(can_use("mystery-license-v3", commercial=True, monthly_active_users=10_000))

t_star = break_even_millions(3000, 0.10, 2.00)
print(f"break-even: {t_star:.0f} million tokens per month")
for volume in (10, 100, 1000, 5000):
    api, own = 2.00 * volume, 3000 + 0.10 * volume
    print(f"{volume:>5} M tokens: API USD {api:>8.0f}   self-host USD {own:>8.0f}   -> {'API' if api <= own else 'self-host'}")
```

Engineering commentary:

- **`classify_release` checks weights first.** If there are no weights, nothing else matters: it is API-only. The `open-source` label requires all three components *and* an approved license. Everything in between is `open-weights`, which is where most real models land. Note that the first example prints `open-weights` even though its license is an approved open-source one (`osi_license` is True). A permissive license on weights alone does not satisfy the strict definition, because the training code and the data information are missing.
- **`.get(...)` with a missing key returns `None`, which counts as false.** The function therefore treats "not stated" the same as "no". When assessing openness, absence of evidence should count against the claim.
- **`can_use` fails closed.** An unrecognised license returns `False` with an instruction to read it. The dangerous alternative, treating an unknown license as permissive, is how teams end up shipping a product on a model they are not allowed to use.
- **The order of checks is deliberate.** Commercial permission is tested before scale limits, because a non-commercial license makes the scale question irrelevant.
- **`break_even_millions` returns `None` when no break-even exists.** Dividing by zero or returning a negative volume would be a silent bug. An explicit `None` forces the caller to handle the case where the API is always cheaper.
- **The table at the end is the decision aid.** A single break-even number is easy to misread. Showing cost at several volumes makes it obvious how far above or below the line you sit, and how sensitive the answer is.

A model-card check is equally small. It reads the metadata header with plain string handling:

```python
def header_keys(card_text):
    """Top-level keys in the metadata block between the first two '---' lines."""
    lines = card_text.splitlines()
    if not lines or lines[0].strip() != "---":
        return {}
    keys = {}
    for line in lines[1:]:
        if line.strip() == "---":
            break
        if ":" in line and not line.startswith((" ", "-")):
            key, value = line.split(":", 1)
            keys[key.strip()] = value.strip()
    return keys

card = """---
license: other
library_name: transformers
---
# Example model
"""
found = header_keys(card)
print(found)
print("custom license without a link" if found.get("license") == "other" and "license_link" not in found else "ok")
```

This is not a full parser for the metadata format, and it does not need to be. It answers the three questions that matter at first glance: is there a license, is it custom, and does the card say where the model came from. You will extend it in the lab.

**Complexity.** Every function here runs in constant time except the header scan, which is linear in the number of lines in the card. The value of the code is not speed. It is that the checks are written down, repeatable, and impossible to skip by accident.

## 4. Practitioner Wisdom & Edge Cases (Reddit / HN / Stack Overflow Synthesis)

**"Open weights" and "open source" are not synonyms.** This is the correction experienced practitioners make most often. If you are writing a proposal, a compliance document, or marketing copy, use "open-weight" unless you have checked the model against the formal definition. Using the wrong term in front of a client's legal team damages your credibility.

**Read the license for the exact repository and version.** Licenses differ between model sizes in one family, between versions of one family, and between the original model and a community fine-tune of it. Gemma's move from custom terms to Apache 2.0 is one example. The reverse also happens: a vendor's newest flagship may be closed even when its earlier models were open.

**A fine-tune inherits obligations.** If a model card lists a `base_model`, the base model's license conditions generally follow the fine-tune. A fine-tune labelled "MIT" by an enthusiast, built on a base model with a restrictive license, does not become MIT because someone typed it into a metadata field.

**"Free" self-hosting is rarely free.** The download costs nothing. The GPU, the electricity, the engineer who gets paged when it falls over, the idle hours when nobody is sending requests, and the work of upgrading to the next model all cost money. People who share real numbers consistently report that staff time, not hardware, dominates.

**Low utilisation destroys the economics.** A GPU busy 5 percent of the time produces tokens that cost twenty times the headline figure. If your traffic is bursty or small, a per-token API almost always wins on cost.

**Self-hosted is not automatically private, and open is not automatically self-hosted.** Running an open-weight model through someone else's hosting service sends your data to that service. Privacy comes from where the computation happens, not from the license.

**Published break-even figures disagree wildly.** Estimates for the volume at which self-hosting pays off range across more than a factor of five between sources, because each assumes different hardware prices, different models, and different utilisation. Treat any single quoted number as an illustration and run the formula with your own inputs.

**Capability gaps close and reopen.** Open-weight models have repeatedly reached the level of the previous year's closed frontier. Whether that is good enough depends on your task. Test on your own examples before deciding. Do not rely on leaderboards.

**Closed models can disappear.** API vendors retire models on a schedule. A workflow tuned carefully for one model version may behave differently on its replacement. With open weights you can keep running the exact version you validated for as long as you like. For regulated or long-lived systems this can outweigh a capability gap.

**Permissive license, unknown data.** Apache 2.0 or MIT on the weights tells you what you may do with the weights. It does not warrant that the training data was collected lawfully. If provenance matters to your client, the data section of the model card is where to look, and silence there is a finding.

## 5. Active Recall Check & Synthesis Summary

**Summary.** AI models are released at three levels: API-only, where you can only call a hosted service; open weights, where you can download and run the parameters; and open source in the strict sense, which requires the weights, the complete code, and detailed information about the training data under terms that permit use, study, modification, and sharing. Most models described as open source are open-weight. The license determines what you may do, and licenses vary between vendors, between models, and between versions. The choice between a hosted API and self-hosting trades capability, convenience, and support against privacy, control, and cost at scale, and the cost question reduces to the break-even volume $T^{*} = F / (c_a - c_s)$, adjusted for utilisation. The model card, read license first, is where all of this is documented.

**Question 1.** A model's weights are published under the Apache 2.0 license. The vendor has not released the training code or any description of the training data. Is the model "open source"? What can you do with it, and what can you not do?

<details>
<summary>View Answer</summary>

Under the Open Source AI Definition it is not open source, because that definition requires the complete training and inference code and detailed information about the training data in addition to the weights. It is an open-weight model with a permissive license. You can download it, run it on your own hardware, fine-tune it, and use it commercially, subject to keeping the license and notices. You cannot see what it was trained on, reproduce the training, or fully audit how it came to behave as it does, and the license gives you no assurance about the provenance of the training data.

</details>

**Question 2.** A startup processes 20 million tokens per month. Self-hosting would cost USD 2,500 per month fixed plus USD 0.10 per million tokens. The API costs USD 3.00 per million tokens. Compute the break-even volume and the monthly cost of each option, and state what non-cost reason could still justify self-hosting.

<details>
<summary>View Answer</summary>

The break-even volume is 2500 divided by (3.00 minus 0.10), which is about 862 million tokens per month. The startup is at 20 million, roughly forty times below that. Its API cost is 20 times 3.00, which is USD 60 per month. Its self-hosting cost is 2,500 plus 20 times 0.10, which is USD 2,502 per month. On cost the API wins overwhelmingly. Self-hosting could still be justified by a requirement that data never leave the company's own machines, by a need to run offline, by a need to pin an exact model version for years, or by a need to fine-tune in ways the API does not allow.

</details>

**Question 3.** You find a fine-tuned model on a public hub. Its card says `license: mit` and `base_model: ` followed by a model that was released under a custom community license with an acceptable use policy. What should you conclude, and what would you check before using it for a client?

<details>
<summary>View Answer</summary>

The MIT label on the fine-tune cannot remove conditions attached to the base model. The fine-tune is a derivative of the base model, so the base model's license terms, including its acceptable use policy and any attribution, naming, or scale conditions, generally still apply. The metadata field reflects what the uploader typed and is not a legal determination. Before using it for a client, read the base model's full license text, confirm that the intended use is commercial-use compatible and within any limits, check whether the base license restricts redistribution of derivatives, and look at the card's sections on training data and intended use. If any of that is unclear, choose a model whose whole lineage is under a permissive license.

</details>

interactiveLab.labTitle: Hands-On Lab: Build a Model Selection Toolkit
interactiveLab.context: A small software company is choosing between calling a hosted AI service and running an open-weight model on its own hardware, and legal has asked whether the model's license even allows the planned use. You will write the checks an engineer runs before committing: classify what a vendor actually released, test a license against the intended use, compute the cost break-even point, and lint a model card for missing information.

Return 'api-only' when there are no weights. Return 'open-source' only when all four are true. Return 'open-weights' in every other case. assert classify_release({"weights": True, "code": True, "data_info": True, "osi_license": False}) == "open-weights", "Without an approved license it is not open-source"
assert classify_release({"weights": True, "code": True, "data_info": False, "osi_license": True}) == "open-weights", "Without data information it is not open-source"
assert classify_release({"weights": True, "code": True, "data_info": True, "osi_license": True}) == "open-source", "All four present is open-source"
print("Step 1 passed: you can tell what a vendor actually released.")

steps.title: Check a license against the intended use
steps.instruction: Implement can_use(license_key, commercial, monthly_active_users). Look the key up in LICENSES and return a tuple (allowed, reason), checking in this order: an unknown key returns (False, 'unknown license: read the full text'); commercial use under a license that forbids it returns (False, 'commercial use is not permitted'); more users than the license's mau_limit returns (False, 'above the monthly-active-user limit: request a license'); otherwise return (True, 'ok'). The function must fail closed: an unrecognised license is never assumed to be permissive. [MOD-1.7]
steps.hintConceptual: A license check is a list of reasons to say no, tried in order. Anything you do not recognise is a no until someone reads the text.
steps.testAssertion:
assert can_use("apache-2.0", True, 5_000_000_000) == (True, "ok"), "Apache 2.0 allows commercial use at any scale"
assert can_use("mit", False, 10) == (True, "ok"), "MIT allows non-commercial use"
assert can_use("research-only", True, 10) == (False, "commercial use is not permitted"), "A research-only license must block commercial use"
assert can_use("research-only", False, 10) == (True, "ok"), "A research-only license allows non-commercial use"
assert can_use("llama-community", True, 700_000_000) == (True, "ok"), "Exactly at the limit is still allowed (the rule is 'more than')"
assert can_use("llama-community", True, 700_000_001) == (False, "above the monthly-active-user limit: request a license"), "Above 700M monthly active users a separate license is required"
assert can_use("totally-new-license", False, 1) == (False, "unknown license: read the full text"), "An unknown license must fail closed"
print("Step 2 passed: unknown licenses fail closed.")

steps.title: Compute the break-even volume
steps.instruction: Implement break_even_millions(fixed_monthly, self_cost_per_m, api_price_per_m). Return fixed_monthly / (api_price_per_m - self_cost_per_m), the monthly volume in millions of tokens at which self-hosting and the API cost the same. If the API price is less than or equal to the self-hosting marginal cost, return None, because the API is then cheaper at every volume. This is the formula T* = F / (c_a - c_s) from Section 2. [MOD-1.7]
steps.hintConceptual: Each million tokens you move from the API to your own server saves the difference between the two per-token prices. The break-even is how many of those savings it takes to pay off the fixed cost.
steps.testAssertion:
_t = break_even_millions(3000, 0.10, 2.00)
assert _t is not None and abs(_t - 1578.9473684) < 1e-6, f"3000 / (2.00 - 0.10) is about 1578.95, got {_t}"
assert abs(break_even_millions(2500, 0.10, 3.00) - 862.0689655) < 1e-6, "2500 / (3.00 - 0.10) is about 862.07"
assert break_even_millions(0, 0.5, 2.0) == 0, "With no fixed cost, self-hosting wins from the first token"
assert break_even_millions(1000, 2.0, 2.0) is None, "Equal marginal prices: no break-even, return None"
assert break_even_millions(1000, 3.0, 2.0) is None, "API cheaper per token: no break-even, return None"
print(f"Step 3 passed: break-even at {_t:.0f} million tokens per month.")

steps.title: Recommend the cheaper option
steps.instruction: Implement cheaper_option(tokens_m, fixed_monthly, self_cost_per_m, api_price_per_m). Compute the API cost as api_price_per_m * tokens_m and the self-hosting cost as fixed_monthly + self_cost_per_m * tokens_m. Return 'self-host' only if it is strictly cheaper, and 'api' otherwise, including on a tie. A single break-even number is easy to misread, so this function answers the question people actually ask: at my volume, which should I pick? [MOD-1.7]
steps.hintConceptual: Total cost is fixed cost plus per-token cost times volume. Compare the two totals. When they are equal, prefer the option with no servers to maintain.
steps.hintSyntax:
api_cost = api_price_per_m * tokens_m
self_cost = fixed_monthly + self_cost_per_m * tokens_m
return "self-host" if self_cost < api_cost else "api"
steps.testAssertion:
assert cheaper_option(10, 3000, 0.10, 2.00) == "api", "At 10M tokens the API (USD 20) beats self-hosting (USD 3001)"
assert cheaper_option(1000, 3000, 0.10, 2.00) == "api", "At 1000M tokens the API (USD 2000) still beats self-hosting (USD 3100)"
assert cheaper_option(5000, 3000, 0.10, 2.00) == "self-host", "At 5000M tokens self-hosting (USD 3500) beats the API (USD 10000)"
assert cheaper_option(1000, 1000, 1.0, 2.0) == "api", "A tie (both USD 2000) should go to the API"
assert cheaper_option(1001, 1000, 1.0, 2.0) == "self-host", "Just past the break-even, self-hosting is strictly cheaper"
assert cheaper_option(10**9, 1000, 3.0, 2.0) == "api", "If the API is cheaper per token it wins at every volume"
print("Step 4 passed: you can turn a volume into a recommendation.")

steps.title: Lint a model card
steps.instruction: Implement lint_model_card(card_text). The metadata header is the block between a first line of '---' and the next '---' line. Collect its top-level keys: lines that contain ':' and do not start with a space or '-'. Return a sorted list of problems: each name in REQUIRED_FIELDS that is missing from the header, plus 'license_link' if the license value is 'other' and there is no license_link key. A card with no header is missing every required field. This automates the first three things to check on any model card. [MOD-1.7]
steps.hintConceptual: You are checking whether the card answers the basic questions: what are the terms, where did this model come from, and what was it trained on. A custom license with no link to its text is a gap too.
steps.testAssertion:
_good = "---
license: apache-2.0
base_model: org/base
datasets:
  - org/data
---
# Model
"
assert lint_model_card(_good) == [], f"A complete header has no problems, got {lint_model_card(_good)}"
_custom = "---
license: other
library_name: transformers
---
# Model
"
assert lint_model_card(_custom) == ["base_model", "datasets", "license_link"], f"Expected ['base_model', 'datasets', 'license_link'], got {lint_model_card(_custom)}"
_linked = "---
license: other
license_link: https://example.com/LICENSE
base_model: org/base
datasets:
  - a
---
"
assert lint_model_card(_linked) == [], "A custom license WITH a license_link is acceptable"
assert lint_model_card("# Just a title
license: mit
") == ["base_model", "datasets", "license"], "With no '---' header every required field is missing, even if 'license:' appears in the body"
_body = "---
license: mit
---
base_model: mentioned only in the body
datasets: also only in the body
"
assert lint_model_card(_body) == ["base_model", "datasets"], "Keys after the closing '---' are body text and must not count"
_nested = "---
license: mit
model-index:
  base_model: nested
  datasets: nested
---
"
assert lint_model_card(_nested) == ["base_model", "datasets"], "Indented (nested) keys are not top-level keys"

interactiveLab.solutionCode:
"""
Lab solution: Build a Model Selection Toolkit
Standard library only.
"""

# License terms used in Step 2. mau_limit is a cap on monthly active users (None = no cap).
LICENSES = {
    "apache-2.0": {"commercial": True, "mau_limit": None},
    "mit": {"commercial": True, "mau_limit": None},
    "llama-community": {"commercial": True, "mau_limit": 700_000_000},
    "research-only": {"commercial": False, "mau_limit": None},
}

# Fields every model card header should have (Step 5).
REQUIRED_FIELDS = ["base_model", "datasets", "license"]


# ---------------------------------------------------------------- Step 1
def classify_release(release):
    """Place a model on the release ladder.

    .get() returns None for a missing key, which is falsy: "not stated" is treated
    as "no". When judging openness, absence of evidence counts against the claim.
    """
    if not release.get("weights"):
        return "api-only"
    if release.get("code") and release.get("data_info") and release.get("osi_license"):
        return "open-source"
    return "open-weights"


# ---------------------------------------------------------------- Step 2
def can_use(license_key, commercial, monthly_active_users):
    """License check that fails closed: an unknown license is never assumed to be fine."""
    terms = LICENSES.get(license_key)
    if terms is None:
        return False, "unknown license: read the full text"
    if commercial and not terms["commercial"]:
        return False, "commercial use is not permitted"
    if terms["mau_limit"] is not None and monthly_active_users > terms["mau_limit"]:
        return False, "above the monthly-active-user limit: request a license"
    return True, "ok"


# ---------------------------------------------------------------- Step 3
def break_even_millions(fixed_monthly, self_cost_per_m, api_price_per_m):
    """T* = F / (c_a - c_s).

    When the API price is not above the self-hosting marginal cost there is no
    break-even. Returning None forces the caller to handle that case explicitly,
    where a division by zero or a negative volume would be a silent bug.
    """
    if api_price_per_m <= self_cost_per_m:
        return None
    return fixed_monthly / (api_price_per_m - self_cost_per_m)


# ---------------------------------------------------------------- Step 4
def cheaper_option(tokens_m, fixed_monthly, self_cost_per_m, api_price_per_m):
    """Compare total monthly cost. A tie goes to the API: same money, no servers to run."""
    api_cost = api_price_per_m * tokens_m
    self_cost = fixed_monthly + self_cost_per_m * tokens_m
    return "self-host" if self_cost < api_cost else "api"


# ---------------------------------------------------------------- Step 5
def lint_model_card(card_text):
    """Flag missing metadata in a model card header.

    Plain string handling is enough for a first-pass check: we only need the
    top-level keys, not a full parse of the metadata format.
    """
    lines = card_text.splitlines()
    keys = {}
    if lines and lines[0].strip() == "---":
        for line in lines[1:]:
            if line.strip() == "---":
                break
            if ":" in line and not line.startswith((" ", "-")):
                key, value = line.split(":", 1)
                keys[key.strip()] = value.strip()

    problems = [field for field in REQUIRED_FIELDS if field not in keys]
    if keys.get("license") == "other" and "license_link" not in keys:
        problems.append("license_link")
    return sorted(problems)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(classify_release({"weights": False}))
    print(classify_release({"weights": True, "osi_license": True}))
    print(classify_release({"weights": True, "code": True, "data_info": True, "osi_license": True}))

    for key, commercial, users in [("apache-2.0", True, 10_000), ("research-only", True, 10_000),
                                   ("llama-community", True, 900_000_000), ("mystery-v3", False, 10)]:
        print(f"{key:>16}: {can_use(key, commercial, users)}")

    t_star = break_even_millions(3000, 0.10, 2.00)
    print(f"break-even: {t_star:.0f} million tokens per month")
    for volume in (10, 100, 1000, 5000):
        print(f"{volume:>5} M tokens per month -> {cheaper_option(volume, 3000, 0.10, 2.00)}")

    card = "---\nlicense: other\nlibrary_name: transformers\n---\n# Example model\n"
    print("card problems:", lint_model_card(card))
